_do_not_edit: Edit stat-names.js and re-run the script. Edits here are overwritten.

targets.name: Targets
targets.plain: How many times the quarterback threw the ball in this player's direction, whether or not he caught it.
targets.why: Catches depend on luck and coverage; being thrown at does not. It is the single most stable sign that a coach trusts a receiver.

receptions.name: Catches
receptions.plain: How many of those passes he actually caught.
receptions.why: In a PPR league each catch is a point on its own, before any yards.

carries.name: Carries
carries.plain: How many times he was handed the ball to run with.
carries.why: Carries near the goal line are where most rushing touchdowns come from, so volume here drives scoring.

pass_attempts.name: Pass attempts
pass_attempts.plain: How many passes the quarterback threw.
pass_attempts.why: A quarterback who throws 40 times has roughly twice the chance to score as one who throws 20, whatever else is true.

target_share.name: Target share
target_share.plain: Of every pass his team threw, the fraction thrown at him. 0.28 means 28 of every 100.
target_share.why: It separates a player who is genuinely first in line from one who happened to get eight targets in a game where his team threw fifty.

air_yards_share.name: Air-yards share
air_yards_share.plain: Of all the yards his team's passes travelled in the air, the fraction that travelled toward him — counting the throw whether or not he caught it.
air_yards_share.why: This is the share of the DOWNFIELD work. A player with a high target share but a low air-yards share is being used on short passes, which caps how big his games can get.

wopr.name: WOPR
wopr.plain: Weighted Opportunity Rating: target share and air-yards share combined into one number, weighted 1.5 to 0.7 in favour of targets.
wopr.why: One number for "how central is he to this passing game", which is the question behind most start/sit and trade decisions.

snap_share.name: Snap share
snap_share.plain: Of his team's offensive plays, the fraction he was on the field for.
snap_share.why: It is the first thing to move when a role changes — a player coming off the field on third down is being phased out before the box score shows it.

first_downs.name: First downs
first_downs.plain: How many of his plays moved the chains.
first_downs.why: Moving the chains keeps his offence on the field, which is how a player gets more chances in the same game.

catch_rate.name: Catch rate
catch_rate.plain: Of the passes thrown at him, the percentage he caught.
catch_rate.why: Read it against how far downfield he plays: 60% on deep throws is excellent and 60% on screens is a problem.

adot.name: aDOT
adot.plain: Average depth of target: how far past the line of scrimmage the ball was thrown, averaged over every pass aimed at him — caught or not.
adot.why: It is the shape of a player, not his quality. A low number means safe and steady; a high one means fewer catches and bigger ones.

racr.name: RACR
racr.plain: Receiver Air Conversion Ratio: the receiving yards he produced for each yard the ball travelled in the air toward him.
racr.why: Above 1 means he is adding yards after the catch beyond what the throw gave him. It is how a short-target player can still be valuable.

pacr.name: PACR
pacr.plain: Passer Air Conversion Ratio: the passing yards a quarterback produced for each yard his throws travelled in the air.
pacr.why: It separates a quarterback whose receivers turn throws into yards from one whose deep balls fall incomplete.

cpoe.name: CPOE
cpoe.plain: Completion Percentage Over Expected: how much more often a quarterback completed a pass than a typical quarterback would have, given the same throws.
cpoe.why: It adjusts for difficulty, so a checkdown artist and a deep thrower can be compared on the same scale.

yac_over_expected.name: YAC over expected
yac_over_expected.plain: Yards after the catch above what a typical receiver would have gained from the same catch in the same situation.
yac_over_expected.why: This is the part of a receiver's production that is him rather than his offence.

separation.name: Separation
separation.plain: How far the nearest defender was when the ball arrived, averaged over his targets.
separation.why: A receiver who cannot get open is one coverage change away from losing his role, however good his box score looks.

cushion.name: Cushion
cushion.plain: How far off him the defender lined up before the snap, averaged over his targets.
cushion.why: A big cushion means defences fear him deep and are conceding the short throw; a small one means the opposite.

rush_yards_over_expected.name: Rush yards over expected per carry
rush_yards_over_expected.plain: Yards gained per carry above what a typical back would have gained with the same blocking and the same defenders in the box.
rush_yards_over_expected.why: It separates the runner from the offensive line, which is the whole question when a back changes teams.

rush_efficiency.name: Rush efficiency
rush_efficiency.plain: How much total distance he travelled, side to side included, for each yard gained downfield.
rush_efficiency.why: A high number means a lot of dancing. It is context for a bad yards-per-carry, not a verdict on its own.

broken_tackles.name: Broken tackles
broken_tackles.plain: How many tackles he made defenders miss.
broken_tackles.why: The clearest sign that a player creates yards his blocking did not give him.

drop_rate.name: Drop rate
drop_rate.plain: The percentage of catchable passes he dropped.
drop_rate.why: Drops are not very repeatable year to year, so a high rate is usually a reason to buy rather than to sell.

yac_per_reception.name: Yards after catch per catch
yac_per_reception.plain: Of his yards, how many came after he caught the ball, per catch.
yac_per_reception.why: It is the half of a receiver's yardage the quarterback did not give him.

ybc_per_reception.name: Yards before catch per catch
ybc_per_reception.plain: Of his yards, how many the ball had already travelled when he caught it, per catch.
ybc_per_reception.why: The companion to the one above: together they say whether a player is a deep threat or a yards-after-catch player.

time_to_throw.name: Time to throw
time_to_throw.plain: How long the quarterback held the ball before releasing it, averaged over his throws.
time_to_throw.why: A quick release protects a bad offensive line and shortens throws; a long one means deep shots and sacks.

aggressiveness.name: Aggressiveness
aggressiveness.plain: The percentage of his throws made into tight coverage, with a defender within a yard of the receiver when the ball arrives.
aggressiveness.why: An aggressive quarterback makes his receivers more valuable and his own completion rate worse.

pressure_rate.name: Pressure rate
pressure_rate.plain: The percentage of his dropbacks on which he was hurried, hit or sacked.
pressure_rate.why: Pressure is the best single predictor of a bad passing day, and it is mostly about the line rather than the quarterback.

on_target_rate.name: On-target rate
on_target_rate.plain: The percentage of his throws that were catchable, ignoring drops and throwaways.
on_target_rate.why: It is completion percentage with the receivers' hands taken out of it.

pocket_time.name: Pocket time
pocket_time.plain: How long he had before the pocket broke down, averaged over his dropbacks.
pocket_time.why: Read alongside time to throw: a quarterback holding the ball longer than his pocket lasts is about to be sacked a lot.

qbr.name: QBR
qbr.plain: ESPN's Total Quarterback Rating: every play a quarterback was involved in, weighted by how much it mattered to winning.
qbr.why: The one quarterback number that accounts for running, sacks and situation rather than passing alone.

fantasy_points.name: Fantasy points
fantasy_points.plain: What he actually scored under this league's scoring.
fantasy_points.why: The outcome. Everything else on this list exists to predict it.

expected_fantasy_points.name: Expected points
expected_fantasy_points.plain: What a typical player would have scored from exactly the same opportunities — the same targets at the same depths, the same carries from the same places on the field.
expected_fantasy_points.why: The gap between this and what he actually scored is the clearest sell-high or buy-low signal there is: opportunity repeats, finishing does not.

epa.name: EPA
epa.plain: Expected Points Added: how much his plays improved his team's chance of scoring, compared with an average play in the same situation.
epa.why: It values a 4-yard gain on third-and-3 above a 9-yard gain on third-and-12, which is what actually happened.

interceptions.name: Interceptions
interceptions.plain: Passes he threw that the defence caught.
interceptions.why: Directly negative in every scoring system, and they end drives that would otherwise have scored.

fumbles_lost.name: Fumbles lost
fumbles_lost.plain: Times he lost the ball and the other team recovered it.
fumbles_lost.why: Negative points, and a back who fumbles twice tends to lose goal-line work.

depth_chart_position.name: Position
depth_chart_position.plain: The position group a player is listed in — quarterback, running back, wide receiver, tight end and so on.
depth_chart_position.why: It decides which slot he can fill in a lineup and who he is actually competing with for the ball. A player listed at one position and used like another is the thing worth noticing, which is why this is stored separately from how he is used.

depth_chart_rank.name: Depth-chart rank
depth_chart_rank.plain: Where he is listed among his own team's players at that position: 1 is the starter, 2 is behind him, and so on.
depth_chart_rank.why: It is the cheapest available signal for whether a player will see the field at all, and it moves before the box score does — a back going from 2 to 1 is next week's volume, visible this week. It is a listing rather than a measurement, so it can be stale or wrong, and snap share is what settles an argument between them.

chance_to_play.name: Chance to play
chance_to_play.plain: How likely this player is to be on the field this week, worked out from the official injury report, beat-reporter signals and his recent snap counts together.
chance_to_play.why: The first question before any lineup decision, and the one the box score cannot answer. Never show it without its basis (below): the same 0.82 can be a measurement or a constant.

availability_basis.name: Chance-to-play basis
availability_basis.plain: Where a chance-to-play number came from. "fitted" means it was measured from this player's own situation; "durability_prior" means it was measured from players like him; "default_durability" means nobody measured anything and a single constant was used.
availability_basis.why: A default_durability number is not a measurement and a claim resting on one has to say so. Kickers and defences always land there, because the availability model covers quarterbacks, running backs, receivers and tight ends only.

not_stored.name: Yards per route run
not_stored.plain: Receiving yards divided by the number of pass routes the player actually ran, rather than by games or by targets.
not_stored.why: It is the best single efficiency number for a receiver, because it counts the plays he was available to be thrown to rather than the plays he was thrown to.
not_stored.needs: A routes-run count per player per week. Nothing in this database has one — not player_week_usage, not nfl_snaps, not the off_* season tables — and it is not derivable from snap counts, because a snap is not a route. It would need a charting feed (PFF, Fantasy Points Data or similar), which is a paid source.

not_stored.name: Touchdown rate
not_stored.plain: The share of a player's touches or targets that ended in a touchdown.
not_stored.why: Touchdown rate swings wildly year to year, so a player far above or below his own history is usually about to move back toward it — which is exactly when to buy or sell him.
not_stored.needs: The pieces exist (touchdowns and touches are both in player_week_usage) but nothing computes or stores the rate, and doing it properly needs red-zone and goal-line touches split out, which this database does not carry. Coach can compute a crude version per player through the ledger; it should not be shown as a stored stat until the red-zone split exists.

not_stored.name: Route participation
not_stored.plain: The share of his team's pass plays on which the player ran a route, rather than blocked or stayed in.
not_stored.why: It is the cleanest early sign that a tight end or a running back has been given a real receiving role.
not_stored.needs: The same routes-run feed as above.

not_stored.name: Red-zone share
not_stored.plain: The share of his team's plays inside the opponent's 20-yard line that went to him.
not_stored.why: Touchdowns come from a small number of plays, and this is the only opportunity measure that counts the plays that score.
not_stored.needs: Play-by-play filtered by field position per player. nfl_play_by_play holds the plays, but nothing aggregates them per player per week, so this is buildable here — it is missing rather than impossible.
